evidence: Three actual timed public-extension/retaining-IJSRuntime/JSRuntime producer deadlines cancel and preserve their actual passed token. Removing the finite CTS would change the token/deadline contract.
Infinity already uses CancellationToken.None without creating a CTS; its cheaper allocation is not an equivalent finite-timeout optimization.
Actual successful timed extension passes a public consumer a never-canceled token; a later original real deadline cancels only its own distinct token.

Separate real public CTS.TryReset/CancelAfter control, consumed by the same actual public IJSRuntime and JSRuntime path, changes an earlier successful retained token when the later call cancels. Its identity is reused; original retained token stays uncanceled.
Public TryReset documentation explicitly warns that components holding an indirect token reference observe the reset source's current state.
limitations: The public CTS control is a compatibility counterexample at the token-consumer/reset boundary, not a compiled shipping timeout-extension candidate or red/green shipped fix.
F097's private nonvirtual default-timeout owner does not imply compatibility for arbitrary public IJSRuntime token consumers.
An owner-specific lifecycle/API redesign is not universally disproved, implemented, benchmarked or implicitly approved.
No sibling constructor/get/set timeout bug is fixed or used as a substitute for this InvokeAsync finding; no browser, JavaScript execution, WebAssembly or application frequency/throughput proof.
timedPlan: One original9-case source sweep only, no source A/B comparison and no performance PR.
